stem: Which of the following best defines growth in plants?
options: A reversible increase in the size of an organ caused by water uptake
An irreversible, permanent increase in the size of an organ or a cell
Any change in the shape of an organ during the life of a plant
An increase in the dry weight of a plant caused only by photosynthesis
explanation: Correct option: (B). Growth is an irreversible permanent increase in size of an organ, its parts or a cell, generally accompanied by metabolic processes. A reversible swelling is not growth, a mere change of shape need not involve any increase in size, and growth is not limited to dry weight gained through photosynthesis.

stem: Plants retain the capacity for unlimited growth throughout their life. This is due to the presence of
options: meristems at certain locations in the plant body
permanent tissues that keep dividing all the time
lignified secondary walls in all mature cells
large central vacuoles in all cells of the body
explanation: Correct option: (A). Meristem cells can divide and self-perpetuate, so new cells are always being added to the plant body (open form of growth). Permanent tissues have lost the capacity to divide, while secondary walls and large vacuoles are features of mature or elongating cells, not of dividing ones.

stem: A dry piece of wood swells when it is placed in water. Why is this swelling NOT regarded as growth?
options: Wood has no cell walls that are able to expand at all
The increase in size is too small to be ever measured
It is reversible and is not driven by metabolism
Swelling happens only in length and never in volume
explanation: Correct option: (C). Growth is an irreversible increase in size that occurs at the expense of metabolic energy. Dead wood merely absorbs water (imbibition); the swelling is reversible and involves no metabolism. Wood does have cell walls, the swelling is measurable, and it is not restricted to length.

stem: Why is no single parameter good enough to demonstrate growth throughout the life of a flowering plant?
options: Growth occurs only in the meristems, which cannot be measured directly
Fresh weight always decreases with age, so it cannot show any growth
Growth stops after flowering, so later stages need no measurement
Parts grow by cell number, size, length or area at different times
explanation: Correct option: (D). Growth is an increase in protoplasm, which is hard to measure directly, so proportional parameters are used, and the right one differs: a maize root apex adds over 17,500 cells per hour (cell number), watermelon cells enlarge up to 3,50,000 times (cell size), a pollen tube is measured by length and a dorsiventral leaf by surface area. Meristem activity can be measured through its products, fresh weight does not always fall with age, and plant growth is indeterminate, not stopped by flowering.

stem: Cells rich in protoplasm, with large conspicuous nuclei and thin cellulosic primary walls with abundant plasmodesmata, belong to which phase of growth?
options: Elongation phase
Meristematic phase
Maturation phase
Differentiation phase
explanation: Correct option: (B). These are the features of constantly dividing cells at the root and shoot apex, i.e., the meristematic phase. Elongation-phase cells show increased vacuolation and enlargement, maturation-phase cells attain maximal size with wall thickening, and differentiation is what happens as cells leave the dividing zone and mature, not a feature of dividing cells.

stem: In arithmetic growth, following a mitotic cell division,
options: both daughter cells continue to divide
neither daughter cell ever divides again
only one daughter cell continues to divide
both daughter cells stop dividing and differentiate
explanation: Correct option: (C). In arithmetic growth only one daughter cell keeps dividing while the other differentiates and matures, giving a linear curve (Lt = L0 + rt). When both daughter cells keep dividing, growth is geometric. If neither divided, or both differentiated, growth by cell division would stop.

stem: A root elongates at a constant rate of 0.8 cm per day. If its length at time zero is 5 cm, what will its length be after 10 days?
options: 8 cm
40 cm
5.8 cm
13 cm
explanation: Correct option: (D). Arithmetic growth follows Lt = L0 + rt = 5 cm + (0.8 cm/day x 10 days) = 5 cm + 8 cm = 13 cm. 8 cm is only the increase (rt), 40 cm wrongly multiplies L0 by r and t, and 5.8 cm adds the growth of just one day.

stem: Cells growing in culture with a limited supply of nutrients are measured over time. Which curve and sequence of phases is expected?
options: Sigmoid curve: lag, then exponential, then stationary phase
Linear curve: one constant rate of increase throughout
J-shaped curve: exponential increase that never slows
Sigmoid curve: exponential, then lag, then stationary phase
explanation: Correct option: (A). Initial growth is slow (lag phase), then rapid (log or exponential phase); with limited nutrients it slows into the stationary phase, giving an S-shaped (sigmoid) curve. A linear curve describes arithmetic growth, an unending J-curve ignores limited nutrients, and the lag phase comes before, not after, the exponential phase.

stem: Leaf A (initial area 5 cm2) and leaf B (initial area 50 cm2) each increase in area by 5 cm2 in the same time. Which statement is correct?
options: Leaf B has the higher relative growth rate, as it is larger
Leaf A has the higher relative growth rate: 100% against 10%
Both have equal relative growth rates, as both gained 5 cm2
Leaf B has the higher relative growth rate: 10 times that of A
explanation: Correct option: (B). Absolute growth rate (5 cm2 in the given time) is the same for both. Relative growth rate expresses growth per unit initial parameter: A = 5/5 = 1 (100%), B = 5/50 = 0.1 (10%), so A grows relatively faster. A larger size or an equal absolute gain does not give a higher or an equal relative rate, and B's relative rate is one-tenth, not ten times, that of A.

stem: The formation of interfascicular cambium from fully differentiated parenchyma cells is an example of
options: differentiation
redifferentiation
dedifferentiation
maturation
explanation: Correct option: (C). Living differentiated cells that had lost the capacity to divide regain it, forming a meristem such as interfascicular cambium or cork cambium; this is dedifferentiation. Differentiation and maturation are the steps by which cells lose the capacity to divide, and redifferentiation is the maturation of the cells produced by such a regained meristem.

stem: During differentiation into a tracheary element, a cell
options: loses protoplasm and forms lignocellulosic secondary walls
keeps its protoplasm and forms thin cellulosic primary walls
develops a large nucleus and dense cytoplasm for division
loses its cell wall and becomes a living conducting cell
explanation: Correct option: (A). To form a tracheary element the cell loses its protoplasm and develops a strong, elastic, lignocellulosic secondary wall to carry water over long distances under extreme tension. Thin primary walls and dense cytoplasm with large nuclei are features of meristematic cells, and a tracheary element is dead with a thick wall, not wall-less.

stem: Cells pushed away from the root apical meristem mature as root-cap cells, while those pushed to the periphery mature as epidermis. What does this show?
options: Root-cap and epidermis come from different meristems
The final structure of a cell depends on its position
Cells from one meristem always share one final structure
Root-cap cells are dedifferentiated epidermis cells
explanation: Correct option: (B). Differentiation in plants is open: cells arising from the same meristem have different structures at maturity, and the final structure is determined by the location of the cell. Both cell types come from the same root apical meristem, cells from one meristem do not all become alike, and root-cap cells are not formed by dedifferentiation of epidermis.

stem: In plant tissue culture, mature leaf parenchyma cells are made to divide and form a callus, which later forms shoots and roots. These two steps represent, in order,
options: differentiation, then dedifferentiation
redifferentiation, then dedifferentiation
dedifferentiation, then redifferentiation
redifferentiation, then differentiation
explanation: Correct option: (C). Mature parenchyma cells that had lost the ability to divide regain it to form the callus (a mass of undifferentiated cells): dedifferentiation. Callus cells then mature into the specialised cells of shoots and roots: redifferentiation. The other orders either start with cells that are already mature becoming more specialised, or reverse the two steps.

stem: Which sequence correctly shows the development of a meristematic cell of a higher plant?

Cell division, maturation, expansion, senescence
Cell division, expansion, maturation, senescence
Maturation, cell division, expansion, senescence

stem: Canary grass coleoptiles bend towards unilateral light. When only the tip is covered with an opaque cap, no bending occurs. What is the best conclusion?
options: The region below the tip perceives light and bends on its own
Light stops cell growth on the shaded side of the coleoptile

stem: In tea plantations the shoot tips are regularly plucked to make the bushes dense. Why does this work?
options: It raises the auxin level in the lateral buds so they grow
It makes the plant produce ABA, which activates lateral buds
It removes the apical bud whose auxin inhibits lateral buds
It stops all cytokinin production so lateral buds can grow
explanation: Correct option: (C). The growing apical bud inhibits lateral (axillary) buds through auxin, a phenomenon called apical dominance. stem: A farmer wants to (i) induce immediate stomatal closure in leaves during a dry spell and (ii) synchronise fruit-set in pineapple. Which PGRs should be used, in that order?
options: Ethylene, then abscisic acid
Cytokinin, then ethylene
Abscisic acid, then gibberellin
Abscisic acid, then ethylene
explanation: Correct option: (D). ABA stimulates stomatal closure, and ethylene is used to initiate flowering and synchronise fruit-set in pineapples. Reversing the order gives each PGR the other's task, cytokinins do not close stomata, and gibberellins are not used to synchronise fruit-set in pineapple.

source.ref: Original practice question (CBSE pattern); NCERT Biology, Class 11, Chapter 13 'Plant Growth and Development'
